title: Today's light and renewal
english: Today the angelic choirs celebrate the praises of God, and the light of Christ's coming shines upon the faithful. Today a joyful spring has dawned for us: Christ, the sun of justice, has shone upon us, bathed us in bright light, and given light to the minds of the faithful.
Today Adam is made new and forms choruses with the Angels, lifted up into heaven. Today the whole world is full of joy at the coming of the Holy Spirit among men.
Today divine grace, the hope of unseen things, shines brightly and lays open before us wonders beyond mind and understanding, and the mystery hidden from eternity.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 9, col. D, to p. 10, col. A (PDF pp. 33-34); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Divina gratia is the subject of both effulget and facit, and miracula and mysterium are both objects of palam facit: divine grace shines out and makes plain to us the wonders that surpass mind and understanding and the mystery hidden from eternity. 'sol iustitiae' = Malachi 4:2 in English Bibles (Malachi 3:20 in the Hebrew/Vulgate numbering), cited. 'spes invisibilium' may recall Romans 8:24-25 or Hebrews 11:1; uncertain, not cited. 'choros agit' rendered 'dances in the choirs' (chorus = choral dance). The illegible margin variant at 'renovatur' was not used.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 9, col. D, to p. 10, col. A (PDF pp. 33-34)
orientation: The preacher opens the homily by proclaiming that the mystery hidden from eternity is now made known.

title: The feast crowns the faithful and fulfills David's oracle; Gabriel announces to Mary
english: Today crowns of enduring virtue are woven. Today God crowns the heads of the benevolent and the devout, of those who zealously keep the feast days, calling lovers of firm faith as ones called and heirs. And the heavenly kingdom zealously summons those who have wisdom for heavenly things to join the divine ministry of the angelic choirs. Today David's oracle is fulfilled, which says: "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult. The fields will be glad, and all the trees of the forest before the face of the Lord, because he comes." David indeed speaks of trees; the Forerunner of the Lord, however, calls them trees producing fruits worthy of repentance, or rather, worthy of the Lord's coming. But our Lord Jesus Christ announces lasting joy to all who believe in him. For he says: "I will see you, and you will rejoice; and no one will take your joy from you." Today the celebrated and ineffable mystery of Christians, who have voluntarily sealed their hope in Christ, is plainly announced to us. Today Gabriel, who stands before God, coming to the most chaste Virgin, announces to her: "Hail, full of grace." She, however, pondering within herself what kind of greeting this might be, the angel immediately adds, saying: "The Lord is with you. Do not fear, Mary; for you have found favor with God. Therefore you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and they will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign in the house of Jacob forever; and there will be no end to his kingdom." Mary said to the angel: "How will this happen to me, since I do not know a man? Will I remain a virgin still? Will the dignity of virginity in me be betrayed and lost?" While the most holy Virgin turned these things over in her mind as if marveling, the angel briefly sets forth the sum of his speech and says: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy one to be born from you will be called Son of God. For what he is, that indeed he will also be called." Accordingly, therefore, holy Mary alone among all generations is chosen by grace.
notes_covered: Opera omnia, Greek and Latin (Paris, 1622), Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 10, cols. A-D (PDF p. 34); Greek column checked on the page image at two places
translator_notes: 'supernumque regnum ... vocat': the Latin allows the kingdom to be either subject or object; the facing Greek makes the kingdom above the subject, and the English follows it. 'Hodie celebre atque ineffabile Christianorum ... mysterium ... adnunciatur': the subject is the mystery. 'sacra ... capita' = 'the sacred heads'. Mary's two further questions after Luke 1:34 are Gregory's expansion, not Scripture. 'solam gratia elegit': grace is the subject of 'chose' (Greek 'he charis exelexato'). 'summa sermonis' = 'the sum of his message'. 'omnino' rendered 'surely'. The Psalm is 95 in the Latin numbering (print margin 'Psal. 95'), Psalm 96 in English Bibles. The Forerunner's 'trees bearing fruit worthy of repentance' is Matthew 3:8-10 (the print's margin reads 'Matth. 4'). 'qui Deo assistit' recalls Luke 1:19, and 'what sort of greeting that was' Luke 1:29. 'ex omnibus generationibus' may echo Luke 1:48; uncertain, not cited. Margin variants not adopted: 'al. ante faciem Domini', 'al. pie ac sancte obsignarunt', 'al. Ecce concipies', 'al. vocabis'.
source_ref: Opera omnia, Greek and Latin (Paris, 1622), Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 10, cols. A-D (PDF p. 34)
orientation: The homilist proclaims that today God crowns the faithful and calls them heirs, fulfills David's prophecy of cosmic joy, cites Jesus' promise of lasting joy, and narrates Gabriel's announcement to Mary and her question, ending with the angel's explanation that the Holy Spirit will overshadow her and the child will be called Son of God.

title: Mary wise where Eve was careless
english: For in truth she was prudent and wise in everything, and no one like her from all generations has ever been found. She was not like Eve before her, a virgin alone in paradise, leading a chorus and dancing, who with her mind grown lax through carelessness received a word from the serpent, the author of all evil. So Eve was corrupted in the judgment of her mind, and through her the deceitful one, pouring out poison and mixing in death, brought them into the whole world, and for this reason all the suffering of the saints came to be. But in the holy Virgin alone Eve's fall was repaired.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 10, col. D, to p. 11, col. A (PDF pp. 34-35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'Non sicut antea virgo Eva ... verbum suscepit' contrasts Mary with Eve; Eve is the subject of suscepit, so it is rendered 'She was not like the virgin Eve of old, who ... received the word', without adding a second receiving by Mary. 'eius lapsus' is ambiguous (Eve's fall, or the fall brought in through her); rendered 'that fall' to keep the ambiguity. Genesis 3:1-6 cited for the serpent and Eve. 'sensu mentis corrupta' may echo 2 Corinthians 11:3 (Vulgate 'corrumpantur sensus vestri ... sicut serpens Evam seduxit'), and death brought into the world may echo Wisdom 2:24 or Romans 5:12; uncertain, not cited. Margin variants 'al. prima virgo' and 'al. mente cordis' not adopted. 'ulla' (feminine) rendered 'no woman'.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 10, col. D, to p. 11, col. A (PDF pp. 34-35)
orientation: The homilist is speaking just after the angel says the Holy Spirit will come upon Mary, and now compares Mary with Eve.

title: Mary questions the gift before accepting it
english: The most holy Virgin did not accept the gift before she had learned who sent it, and what the gift was, and who bore it. She weighed the matter within herself, and spoke as if hesitating, and said to the angel: "From where have you brought us this blessing in this way? From what kind of storehouse has this pearl of the word been sent out to us? From where has the gift drawn its substance for us? You have come from heaven, yet you walk upon the earth. You wear a human form, yet you shine with the brightness of light."
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, cols. A-B (PDF p. 35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: The Virgin's questions are the author's expansion of the scene, not a Gospel quotation, so nothing is cited. 'Unde nobis donum materiam paravit?' is obscure (literally 'whence has the gift prepared matter for us?'); rendered close to the letter as 'made ready its substance'. The margin variant 'al. promissum' (perhaps 'promissum' for 'donum', 'the promise') was not adopted. 'addidicisset' as printed (from addisco). 'et ... resplendes' rendered 'yet you shine' to bring out the contrast set up by the previous clause.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, cols. A-B (PDF p. 35)
orientation: Mary speaks to Gabriel in the Annunciation dialogue, asking where his blessing comes from before she receives it.

title: Do not fear, grace is not measured by nature
english: While the most holy Virgin was turning these things over within herself, the Archangel resolved her questioning with words such as these. He said to her: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35). And so the holy child to be born of you will also be called Son of God (Luke 1:35). And do not fear, Mary, for I have come not to strike fear into you but to drive the cause of fear away from you. Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God (Luke 1:30). Do not judge grace according to nature, for grace does not allow itself to be made subject to the laws of nature."
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, cols. B-C (PDF p. 35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Ib. Luc. 1': Luke 1:35 and Luke 1:30. Section 1 renders 'gratiam apud Deum' as 'favor with God'; here 'grace with God' is used because the next two sentences play on gratia ('do not judge grace by nature'), and 'favor' would break the link. The first 'Et ne timeas Maria' opens the author's own expansion and is left uncited; the full clause 'Ne timeas Maria: invenisti enim gratiam apud Deum' carries the citation. Margin variant 'al. legi' (singular 'law') not adopted; it does not change the sense.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, cols. B-C (PDF p. 35)
orientation: Gabriel answers Marys question by saying the Holy Spirit will come upon her and the child will be called Son of God.

title: Mary alone learns what prophets never knew
english: Mary, you know what lay hidden from the patriarchs and prophets. Virgin, you have learned what remained hidden even from the angels. Most holy one, you have heard what the chorus of those breathed upon by the divine Spirit never merited to hear. Moses and David, Isaiah and Daniel, and all the prophets proclaimed him, yet they did not know the manner or the reason.

But you alone, most holy Virgin, now receive the mysteries unknown to all of them, and you understand their cause. For where the Holy Spirit is, everything is accomplished swiftly and without hesitation. Where divine grace is present, all things are possible with God.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, cols. C-D (PDF p. 35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'omnia Deo sunt possibilia': the wording matches Matthew 19:26 / Mark 10:27, while the Annunciation context points to the angel's word in Luke 1:37; both cited inline, Mark 10:27 left in this note. 'Quae adhuc Angelis etiam fuerunt abscondita' may recall 1 Peter 1:12 or Ephesians 3:9-10; uncertain, not cited. 'divino spiritu afflatorum chorus' rendered 'the choir of those inspired by the divine Spirit' (the inspired prophets; 'divino spiritu' kept, capitalised because it is the Spirit of God). Margin variant 'al. suscipe et intellige' (imperatives: 'receive and understand') not adopted; the print's indicatives fit 'nunc' and the run of the passage.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, cols. C-D (PDF p. 35)
orientation: Gabriel is still answering Mary after telling her the Holy Spirit will come upon her.

title: The Holy Spirit and the Son of God
english: Gabriel went on: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy child to be born from you will be called Son of God" (Luke 1:35). If he is Son of God, he is also God, of the same form as the Father and coeternal with him. In him the Father holds all brightness. He is the imprint and image in person, and glory shines forth through his radiance.

Just as rivers come forth from an everlasting spring, so from this everlasting and ever-living spring comes forth the everlasting and true light of the world, Christ our God. For about him the Prophets cried out, 'The rush of the river gladdens the city of God' (Psalms 46:4). It gladdens not one city alone, but all cities. For as it gladdens one city, it gladdens the whole world.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, col. D, to p. 12, col. A (PDF pp. 35-36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 45' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 45:5 = Psalm 46:4 in English Bibles; English numbering used in the citation. 'character atque imago in persona ... per splendorem gloria' reflects Hebrews 1:3 (Greek charakter tes hypostaseos, apaugasma tes doxes); cited. 'imago' may also recall Colossians 1:15 and 'eiusdem formae' Philippians 2:6; not cited separately. 'clarificatio' rendered 'glory'. 'in persona' rendered 'in His own person' rather than 'of His person', which would import Hebrews 1:3 wording the Latin does not have; 'per splendorem gloria refulget' kept as 'through the radiance the glory shines out' (no added 'through Him, as'). 'vera lux mundi' joins John 1:9 (true light) and John 8:12 (light of the world); both cited. The ascription 'De eo namque Prophetae clamarunt' is plural in the print and kept as 'the prophets'.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, col. D, to p. 12, col. A (PDF pp. 35-36)
orientation: Gabriel is still speaking to Mary, explaining who the child to be born will be.

title: Mary alone bears all grace
english: So it was fitting that the angel should address his foretelling first of all to the holy virgin Mary: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord with you” (Luke 1:28). For the whole treasure of grace had been stored away with her.

For out of all generations this virgin alone has stood forth holy in body and in spirit, and she alone bears him who by his word bears all things. Not only does the bodily beauty of this most holy one fill us with wonder, but the virtues of her soul do as well.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, cols. A-B (PDF p. 36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'sancta corpore et spiritu' matches the Vulgate of 1 Corinthians 7:34, said of the unmarried virgin; cited. 'qui verbo omnia portat' matches Hebrews 1:3 ('portansque omnia verbo virtutis suae'); cited. 'praesignificavit' with 'primo omnium' rendered 'announced first of all'. Margin variant 'al. Archangelus' not adopted. 'cum ipsa' and 'eum' are read from the page image, where c and e look alike in this typeface.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, cols. A-B (PDF p. 36)
orientation: The preacher goes on to explain why Gabriel greeted Mary as he did.

title: The Lord with Mary and not an earthly bridegroom
english: For this reason too, Gabriel first greeted her and spoke to her with those words: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you" (Luke 1:28). The one with you is no earthly bridegroom, but the Lord himself of sanctification, the Father of chastity, the Author of incorruption, and the Giver of freedom. He is the Steward of salvation, and the Keeper and Giver of true peace. He made man from virgin earth, and from his side and rib he took Eve. This Lord is with you, and he is also from you.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, cols. B-C (PDF p. 36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'sanctificationis Dominus' rendered 'the Lord of holiness'; the same choice is used for sanctificatio in section 13 (margin variant 'al. sanctitatis', 'holiness', gives the same sense). 'pater castitatis' kept lower-case, as in the print: a title of the Lord, not the First Person. 'ex terra virgine creavit hominem' alludes to Genesis 2:7 (Adam from untilled earth) and 'ex illius latere ac costa Evam' to Genesis 2:21-22; both cited. 'rursum ex te' rendered 'in turn comes from you'. Margin variant 'al. protulit, creavit' at 'assumpsit' not adopted.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, cols. B-C (PDF p. 36)
orientation: The preacher explains to his hearers what Gabriel meant when he said the Lord is with Mary.

title: Joining the angel's greeting to Mary
english: Come now therefore, dearest ones, and let us follow the angels in their praise. As grateful people, let us pay what we owe with all our strength, saying: "Hail and rejoice, full of grace, the Lord is with you" (Luke 1:28).

For to be hailed and to rejoice is truly yours, because divine grace has chosen to dwell with you, as it knows: with a maidservant is the King of glory; with the beautiful one is he who is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men (Psalms 45:2); with the undefiled one is he who sanctifies all things. God is with you, and God is from you, and perfect man, in whom all the fullness of deity dwells (Colossians 2:9).
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, cols. C-D (PDF p. 36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 44' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 44:3 = Psalm 45:2 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. 'in quo omnis plenitudo divinitatis inhabitat' quotes Colossians 2:9; cited. 'Tuum ... est avere, atque gaudere' plays on Ave (from avere, 'to fare well'); rendered 'to fare well and to rejoice'. 'Rex gloriae' may recall Psalm 24:7-10 and 'ancilla' Luke 1:38; stock titles here, not cited. 'debitum ... grati' rendered 'the debt of thanks' (margin 'al. grato animo', 'with a grateful heart', gives the same sense).
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, cols. C-D (PDF p. 36)
orientation: The preacher now exhorts the congregation to take up Gabriel's greeting to Mary after recounting that the Lord is with her.

title: Hail to Mary as light and fruitful field
english: Hail, full of grace, fount of light, who enlightens all who believe in him. Hail, full of grace, rising of the sun known to the mind, and undefiled flower of life. Hail, full of grace, most fragrant meadow. Hail, full of grace, vine always thriving, who fills with joy the souls of those who glorify you.

Hail, full of grace, field never plowed yet bringing forth the most beautiful fruit. By nature you brought forth fruit in our human way, keeping the full time of stirring and bearing. Yet this was beyond nature, or rather above nature, for the divine Word came from above and made Adam anew in your holy womb. The Holy Spirit granted fruitfulness to the holy virgin, and the true body was taken from her body.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, col. D, to p. 13, col. A (PDF pp. 36-37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Second paragraph opens 'Your bearing was according to nature' to carry the elliptical 'Secundum naturam quidem ... protulisti' as a full sentence; it supplies no new idea beyond protulisti. 'tempore motus, gestationisque servato' (as printed) rendered 'keeping the time of the child's stirring and of carrying'; 'the child's' makes explicit what motus means here (the sense of motus here is uncertain). 'quidem ... autem' pairs fecunditatem with corpus, so 'verum' is taken as the adjective ('the true body'), not as the conjunction 'but'. 'intelligibilis solis oriens' rendered 'dawning of the spiritual Sun' (intelligibilis = known by the mind, not the visible sun); the partly legible margin variant ('solis iustitiae'?) not adopted. 'fons lucis, qui ... illuminat' keeps the print's third person; 'in ipsum' = Christ. No Scripture cited: the titles are the author's own images.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, col. D, to p. 13, col. A (PDF pp. 36-37)
orientation: The homily continues praising Mary with a series of greetings after Gabriel announces the conception to her.

title: Christ the pearl from two natures
english: As the pearl comes from two natures, from lightning indeed and from water, by certain hidden indications and signs in the sea, so also our Lord Jesus Christ comes forth without confusion and without change from the pure, chaste, undefiled, and holy virgin Mary. He is perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity, like the Father in all things and of the same substance with us in all things, yet free from all sin.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, cols. A-B (PDF p. 37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'nobis per omnia consubstantialis, sed omnis peccati expers' echoes Hebrews 4:15 ('tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin'); cited. The two-natures formula (inconfuse, immutabiliter, perfect in Godhead and manhood, consubstantial with us) is post-Chalcedonian language and supports the later dating noted in the book's description. 'patri per omnia similis' confirmed on the page image (printed p. 13 col. A; lower-case 'patri' as the print writes 'pater' throughout). 'consubstantialis' kept as the exact doctrinal term 'consubstantial'. 'occultis quibusdam indiciis ac signis maris provenit' rendered close to the letter ('arising through certain hidden tokens and signs of the sea'; maris goes with signis); the sense is the ancient belief that pearls form from lightning striking the sea. The margin note on Ephrem's sermon on the pearl is an editor's cross-reference and was not translated.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, cols. A-B (PDF p. 37)
orientation: The homilist is still explaining how Jesus took a true human body from Mary after the account of Gabriel's announcement.

title: Many longed to see him, Mary alone received him
english: Very many of the holy fathers, patriarchs, and prophets longed to see him and to stand as witnesses in his presence, but they could not. Some of them glimpsed him only through visions, in shadowy outline and in riddles. Others heard the divine voice from the pillar of cloud and were granted sights of holy angels.

But to Mary alone, the holy virgin, Gabriel the Archangel came in bright light, announcing to her, "Hail, full of grace" (Luke 1:28). So she received the Word, and in the time of bodily completion she brought forth the precious Pearl.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, cols. B-C (PDF p. 37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'desiderarunt eum videre ... et non potuerunt' echoes Matthew 13:17 / Luke 10:24; cited. 'in columna nubis divinam vocem audierunt' matches the Vulgate of Psalm 98:7 ('in columna nubis loquebatur ad eos'), which is Psalm 99:7 in English Bibles; English numbering cited (compare Exodus 33:9). 'adumbratim in aenigmatibus' may recall Numbers 12:8 or 1 Corinthians 13:12; uncertain, not cited. 'Patrum' rendered lower-case 'fathers' (the Old Testament fathers, not God the Father). 'Pearl' capitalised as a title of Christ, continuing section 11. Margin variants 'al. in aenigmate' and 'al. Angelus' not adopted.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, cols. B-C (PDF p. 37)
orientation: The preacher contrasts the patriarchs and prophets who only glimpsed the coming Lord with Mary to whom Gabriel came.

title: Call to sing of the Lord entering his rest
english: So come, you also, my beloved, and let us sing those sweet words set before us from the spiritual harp of David, saying: "Rise up, Lord, to your resting place, you and the ark of your sanctification" (Psalm 132:8). For the most holy Virgin is truly that ark, gilded within and without, who received the whole treasure of sanctification.
Rise up, Lord, to your resting place. Rise up, Lord, from the bosom of the Father, to lift up the fallen race of the first parent.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, cols. C-D (PDF p. 37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 131' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 131:8 = Psalm 132:8 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. The Latin 'arca sanctificationis tuae' is translated from the sermon's text ('ark of Your holiness'), not from the Hebrew-based English ('ark of Your might'). 'intrinsecus et extrinsecus deaurata' alludes to the ark overlaid with gold inside and out (Exodus 25:11); cited. 'ex sinu Patris' takes its phrase from John 1:18; cited. sanctificatio rendered 'holiness', as in section 8.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, cols. C-D (PDF p. 37)
orientation: After recounting Gabriel coming to Mary, the preacher now urges the hearers to sing David's oracle about the Lord and the ark.

title: David addresses the daughter about the king
english: As he requested this and earnestly entreated for it, David spoke in prophecy to the branch that would spring from him bearing the flower of that most beautiful fruit, saying: "Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty, for he himself is the Lord your God, and you will worship him" (Psalm 45:10-11).

David continues: "Listen, daughter, to what was foretold about you before, so that you may see the realities themselves with the eyes of knowledge. Listen to me, who foreshadows this for you, and to the Archangel, who clearly announces to you the perfect mysteries."
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, col. D, to p. 14, col. A (PDF pp. 37-38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 44' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 44:11-12 = Psalm 45:10-11 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. The rod that puts forth a flower is Isaiah 11:1 (Vulgate 'egredietur virga de radice Iesse et flos de radice eius ascendet'); cited here and in section 15. 'rex' capitalised as King because the verse goes on 'He is the Lord your God'. 'in te praedicta' rendered 'foretold of you'. 'perfecta mysteria' rendered 'the mysteries fulfilled' (perfectus as accomplished). The faint margin note at 'adorabis eum' ('al. dele...'?) was not used.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, col. D, to p. 14, col. A (PDF pp. 37-38)
orientation: David the prophet is speaking in prophecy to the branch that is to bring forth the fruit, continuing the appeal to honor the Virgin.

title: Call to praise the branch from Jesse
english: Come, therefore, beloved, and as we call to memory what has gone before, let us glorify that branch from Jesse, sprouting so wonderfully and beyond all telling (Isaiah 11:1). Let us praise it together, let us proclaim it blessed, and let us receive it with joyful acclamations.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, col. A (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'virgam ... ex Iesse ... germinantem' alludes to Isaiah 11:1; cited. 'beatam praedicemus' may echo Luke 1:48 ('all generations will call me blessed'); possible, not cited. The rod (virga, feminine) stands for Mary; 'it' keeps the image as the print has it.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 14, col. A (PDF p. 38)
orientation: The preacher now addresses the congregation after quoting David's prophecy and urges them to praise Mary as the branch from Jesse.

title: Joseph and pregnant Mary register at Bethlehem and she gives birth
english: For Luke bears witness in the divine Gospels not to Joseph alone but also to Mary the bearer of God. Looking back to the very house and lineage of David, he relates the story and says:

"Joseph went up from Galilee to a city of Judea called Bethlehem, in order that he might be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant, since they themselves were of the house and family of David (Luke 2:4-5). And it happened that while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her son the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15). She wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn (Luke 2:6-7)."
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, cols. A-B (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margins 'Luc. 2', 'Ibidem': Luke 2:4-7. 'primogenitum omnis creaturae' is the author's blend of Luke 2:7 ('firstborn son') with Colossians 1:15 ('firstborn of all creation'); rendered once as 'her son, the firstborn of all creation' and cited to Colossians 1:15 beside the clause. The print puts the Bethlehem clause before 'because they were of the house ... of David'; that order is kept. 'Dei genitrix' rendered 'Mother of God' (Theotokos). Margin variant 'al. solum' at 'soli' not adopted. 'pannis' rendered 'cloths' to keep it distinct from 'fasciis' ('swaddling bands') in section 17.

orientation: The homilist narrator cites Luke's Gospel to place Joseph and Mary of David's house at Bethlehem for the birth.

title: The Creator wrapped in cloths and laid in a manger
english: She wrapped him in swaddling bands, him who is clothed with light as with a garment (Psalm 104:2). She wrapped in rags him who formed all creation. She laid him in a manger, him who sits upon the cherubim and is praised by countless angels (Luke 2:7). The divine Word rested in the manger of unreasoning animals, so that to human beings made truly unreasoning by their own free will he might grant reasoning understanding. In the feeding trough of beasts the heavenly bread was set forth, to make men unreasoning like cattle partakers of mystical food.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, cols. B-C (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margins 'Psal. 103' and 'Psal. 79' are Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 103:2 = Psalm 104:2 and Vulgate Psalm 79:2 = Psalm 80:1 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. Margin 'Dan. 7': Daniel 7:10 (thousands upon thousands serving Him). 'Fasciis eum' read for the print's 'Fasciis cum' (an evident misprint: the verb needs an object, and the next two sentences repeat 'eum'). The wordplay irrationalis / rationalis is kept as 'without reason' / 'a sense of reason'. 'redderet' has no expressed subject (the Word or the bread, which here is Christ); an infinitive of purpose ('to make') keeps that open. 'caelestis panis' may recall John 6:51 and 'instar pecorum' Psalm 49:12 (Vulgate 48:13); uncertain, not cited. Margin variant 'al. panis vitae appositus est' not adopted.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 14, cols. B-C (PDF p. 38)
orientation: The narrator describes Mary wrapping the newborn child and laying him in the manger of animals.

title: No place in the inn
english: And there was not even a place for them in the inn (Luke 2:7). He who built heaven and earth by his word had no place. For though he was rich, he became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9). He chose extreme lowliness for the salvation of our nature, out of his innate goodness toward us.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, cols. C-D (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margins 'Gen. 1' and '2. Cor. 8': creation by the word (Genesis 1, cited at 1:1 for 'heaven and earth') and 2 Corinthians 8:9. The opening sentence repeats Luke 2:7; cited. 'ingenita sua ... bonitate' rendered 'the goodness toward us that is His by nature' (ingenitus = inborn, innate). Creation by the word may also recall Psalm 33:6; not cited separately.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 14, cols. C-D (PDF p. 38)
orientation: The homilist continues the birth narrative after the laying of the child in the manger.

title: The manger as a royal and cherubic throne
english: He who fulfilled all forethought and ordering of the hidden mysteries of the dispensation rested in a manger: in heaven in the bosom of the Father (John 1:18), and in a cave in the arms of his mother. Angelic choirs encircled him, singing glory in heaven and proclaiming peace on earth (Luke 2:14).

In heaven he sat at the right hand of the Father, and in the manger he rested as upon the Cherubim. For even this was truly a Cherubic throne, a royal throne, a holy of holies, alone glorious on earth and holier than the saints, in which Christ our God rested. To him be glory and honor and dominion, with the most spotless Father and the most holy and life giving Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, Amen.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, col. D, to p. 15, col. A (PDF pp. 38-39); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'gloriam ... pacem' alludes to the angels' song in Luke 2:13-14; cited. 'a dextris Patris sedebat' is stock creedal language (compare Psalm 110:1; Hebrews 1:3) and 'super Cherubim' recalls Psalm 80:1, cited in section 17; neither cited again here. 'in sinu Patris' recalls John 1:18, cited in section 13. The sentence 'Qui ... implevit ... in praesepio requievit' has two verbs on one relative; rendered as one sentence with 'He who carried out ... rested in the manger', the two 'in heaven ... in the cave' phrases standing between them as in the Latin. 'Thronus ... et hic erat' taken with hic as the pronoun ('this too was a throne'); 'here too' would also fit. 'immaculatissimo Patre' rendered 'the all-pure Father'. 'in spelunca' (the cave of the Nativity) is the author's, not Luke's. 'super' and 'in quo' are damaged in the print (printed p. 15) and are supplied from the visible letters; the margin variant 'al. occulto dispensationis mysterio' not adopted.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 14, col. D, to p. 15, col. A (PDF pp. 38-39)
orientation: The preacher is closing the homily at the birth in the cave and manger described just before.
